source_review.notes: Reviewed all ten references. Reactor/proactor foundations were checked against Schmidt and POSA2. Current task/microtask behavior was checked against the WHATWG living standard; loop/worker ownership against current libuv 1.x design; readiness and edge-trigger guidance against Linux man-pages 6.18; completion against Microsoft IOCP; and runtime blocking/fairness against current Node documentation. Runtime-specific orders are not generalized.

evidence: Definitions and Notation defines e_i, s_i, f_i, L_i, C_i, R_i, B, c, k, O, and K before mathematical use.
Lifecycle state/generation arrows and outstanding-capacity bounds are directionally and semantically consistent.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Timing, chunk, and ownership notation was reviewed; eligibility, start, service, response, and quiescence are not conflated.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/CONPAR-031/report.json records two tasks, two microtasks before the timer, and four callbacks in the expected order.
The callback trace was manually replayed: io-ready queues parse/authorize, checkpoint drains both, then timer runs.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Queue indices, counts, and exact stdout were independently recomputed and agree.

evidence: For c>0 and callback budget B, k<=floor(B/c) follows from kc<=B under the constant-cost estimate.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The chapter labels the chunk calculation as an initial estimate and does not promote it to a worst-case timing proof.

evidence: Reviewed empty/ready descriptors, partial I/O, would-block, edge/level trigger, hot descriptor quotas, recursive microtasks, zero-delay timers, and callback overrun.
Reviewed pool saturation, synchronous reentrancy, generation reuse, cancel/complete races, close, every shutdown state, multi-loop routing, adversarial input, MMIO, and real-time transfer.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Boundary review covers scheduling, I/O, queueing, state, lifetime, overload, failure, topology, and physical-system limits.

evidence: Outstanding ownership is bounded by 0<=|O|<=K, reserved before submission and released exactly once at terminal transfer.
Callbacks have work limits; descriptor readiness persists logically across fairness yields; state/generation is revalidated after every suspension.
invariant_checking.notes: The ownership and progress invariants were reviewed across success, partial progress, cancellation, late completion, close, overload, and shutdown.

evidence: The run-to-completion argument correctly supplies serialization only within one callback segment and explicitly reopens interleaving after suspension.
The starvation argument identifies unbounded segment or self-replenishing priority work as removing a response bound for competing eligible callbacks.
proof_review.notes: The chapter proves design implications under stated scheduler policies and does not claim universal runtime fairness or hard real-time bounds.

evidence: Abstract loop phases are explicitly separated from WHATWG, libuv, Node, browser, Python, Rust, and OS-specific behavior.
Executable limitations state that the FIFO checkpoint model proves no fairness, latency, or actual I/O behavior.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Specification guarantees, abstract mechanisms, deterministic traces, empirical budgets, and safety-critical claims remain distinct.

evidence: python3 tools/verify_snippets.py CONPAR-031 passed the one executable queue model with exact output and empty stderr.
Callback cost, chunk size, lag, pool saturation, target timer behavior, and hardware timing are explicitly empirical.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The Python run validates one stipulated queue policy only and makes no production-runtime performance claim.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed distinctions among concurrency/parallelism, run-to-completion/suspension, readiness/completion, reactor/proactor, task/microtask, blocking/offload, fairness/ordering, responsiveness/readiness, and cancellation/completion. Ownership connects registration to terminal cleanup.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed edge-trigger drain rules, fairness quotas, callback budgets, monotonic timers, file/DNS/crypto pools, CPU chunking, bounded queues, generation checks, cancellation races, graceful shutdown, loop sharding, instrumentation, adversarial complexity, and target review boundaries.

pedagogical_review.notes: The one-page review is a dense operational reference; exposition builds from the loop mechanism through queues, I/O, work, lifecycle, and operations; ten examples are distinct; exercises progress from retrieval through industrial transfer with complete answers.

limitations: Internal authoring and verification evidence only; no external runtime, operating-system, academic, practitioner, clinical, controls, hardware, security, regulatory, real-time, or functional-safety review is claimed. The queue model does not execute a real event loop, I/O, workers, cancellation, shutdown, timing, or deployment behavior.
